p.title: How a scientific idea improves
p.challenge: Press Next. At the question, choose "No" to see how science changes when new evidence appears

nodes.text: Scientists hold an idea based on evidence
nodes.info: Long ago many people believed the Earth was the centre of everything.
The telescope and the microscope let people see things they could never see before.

nodes.text: Does the new evidence fit the idea?
nodes.info: Scientific ideas stand or fall on evidence, not on opinion or age.
Keep the idea, keep checking it. An idea that fits all the evidence is kept, but scientists go on testing it.
Scientists test and check the new evidence carefully. Scientists repeat observations to be sure they are right.
Improve or replace the idea. Careful observations showed that the Earth and the planets go around the Sun. In 2006, Pluto was placed in a new group: dwarf planets.
Every answer leads to new questions. Science is never finished, so it keeps growing.

events.label: C.V. Raman discovers the Raman effect
events.info: 28 February 1928, a special scattering of light. We celebrate 28 February as National Science Day.

events.label: Raman wins the Nobel Prize in Physics
events.info: The first Asian to win a Nobel Prize in science.

events.label: Chandrayaan-3 lands near the Moon's south pole
events.info: 23 August 2023: a big ISRO team of many kinds of scientists made it happen.

p.title: Inquiry: finding out step by step
p.challenge: Meena wants to know if salt makes ice melt faster. Arrange her inquiry steps in order

nodes.info: Curiosity starts with noticing something.

nodes.text: Ask: does salt make ice melt faster?
nodes.info: A question you can test.
A guess that a test can check.
Plan a fair test with two ice cubes. Same size of cube, same place, same time. Only one cube gets salt.
Is ONLY the salt different? In a fair test you change only one thing. Salt in the sun and no salt in the shade is NOT fair.
Do the test and record what really happens. Write down the true result, even if it surprises you.
Repeating shows the result is not just luck.
Does the result support the hypothesis?

p.title: Metal or non-metal? Test a lump
p.challenge: A shopkeeper tests a shiny lump. Press Next and choose each test result to see what it tells you

nodes.text: Take an unknown lump of material
Shiny when freshly cut or polished?
nodes.info: Lustre: metals are shiny.
Hammer it: does it spread into a thin sheet? Malleable: like aluminium foil and silver vark. Brittle solids like sulphur and coal break into powder.
Sonorous: that is why bells are made of metal.
Metals are also ductile (drawn into wires) and good conductors of heat and electricity.
Non-metals are usually dull, brittle, not sonorous and poor conductors (exceptions: iodine is shiny, graphite conducts).

Melt the ice, then cool the water until it freezes back to ice. No new substance forms, so this is a physical change

p.title: Will this iron nail rust?
p.challenge: Nail A is in dry air, nail B is in boiled water under oil, nail C is in a little water open to air. Press Next and answer for each nail

nodes.info: Nail A is kept with a drying agent, so it has no moisture.
Nail B: boiling removes air from the water and the oil layer stops new air getting in.
Rust is a reddish-brown substance, iron oxide. Iron + oxygen + water → rust. This is a chemical change; rust flakes off and fresh iron below rusts too.
Without either air or water, iron does not rust.
Paint, oil or grease, galvanise (coat with zinc) or use stainless steel. These keep air and water away from the iron.

p.title: Conduction, convection or radiation?
p.challenge: Pick an example, like the Sun warming your face or water circulating in a pan. Press Next and answer the questions to find how the heat travels

nodes.text: Heat moves from a hotter place to a colder one
Does it need any material in between?
nodes.info: The Sun's heat crosses empty space to reach the Earth.
Sun's heat through space; warmth in front of a fire or heater. Dark surfaces absorb more of it.
Does the material itself move? In liquids and gases, warm parts rise and cool parts sink.
Water circulating in a heated pan; warm air rising from a stove and out of a high ventilator.
Particle to particle while the material stays in place, like the handle of a steel ladle getting hot.

nodes.text: Land and sea side by side

nodes.info: Land heats up faster than the sea.
Air above the hot land warms and rises.
Cooler air from over the sea moves in towards the land.
Land cools down faster than the sea.
Air above the warmer sea rises.
Cooler air from the land moves out to the sea.

p.title: What gas does a plant give out?
p.challenge: Plants respire day and night. Press Next and choose Day or Night to see which gas the plant gives out

nodes.text: Every living part of the plant respires
nodes.info: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and seeds break down food using oxygen to release energy.
Photosynthesis AND respiration happen. Photosynthesis makes more oxygen than the plant uses.
The plant gives out OXYGEN.
Only respiration happens. With no light there is no photosynthesis.
The plant gives out carbon dioxide.

p.title: Which eclipse is it?
p.challenge: Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line. Press Next and choose which body is in the middle

nodes.text: Sun, Earth and Moon line up
nodes.info: This does not happen every month, because the Moon's path is slightly tilted.

nodes.text: Which body is in the middle?

nodes.info: The Moon's shadow falls on the Earth. It can happen only on a new moon day.
Never look at the Sun directly, even during a solar eclipse. Use certified solar eclipse glasses.
The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can happen only on a full moon night. In a total lunar eclipse the Moon often looks reddish.
A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes.
